transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Atlas Health - Head of ML), Sara O'Neil (Atlas - SRE), Ben Torres (Atlas - Security)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex Chen from Redwood, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. Today we'll run through the console tracing, error analysis and request logs, and show a typical debugging flow for a model-serving incident.
[00:12] Marcus: Thanks Alex, excited — we've got Sara and Ben on from infra/security. High level, we're looking at how fast we can find root cause for failed responses and PS — latency spikes.
[00:20] Priya: Great. Quick agenda, tracing overview, then request logs and retention, error analysis UI, and then a live debugging demo with a sample trace. We'll also touch on retention/redaction and how this works in Dedicated / VPC.
[00:35] Sara: Quick Q up front — do you keep raw request payloads by default? We need to understand PII exposure and retention.
[00:40] Alex: Short answer: retention is configurable. By default hosted keeps 30 days, but in Dedicated/VPC you can disable request payloads and ship only metadata, or use field-level redaction and KMS. We'll send SOC2 and KMS docs after.
[00:55] Ben: And you support BYOK with HSM?
[00:58] Priya: Yes, BYOK via Cloud KMS or an HSM-backed solution, and audit logs go to the control plane but can be forwarded to your SIEM. There's a small note, sometimes the agent transcription says 'K V cash' which is our KV cache, sorry for the mis-speech in notes.
[01:15] Marcus: ha ok. Let's jump to tracing.
[01:20] Priya: (screen share) Here's the tracing dashboard. Each trace maps to a request id — you can filter by model, route, and status. We capture timing for key spans: request ingress, routing, model invoke, KV cache hit/miss, and token generation.
[01:35] [Priya clicks through] You can see a trace with a 1.2s token gen but a routing delay of 700ms — that was due to cold connection to a dedicated pool. We also annotate traces with the model variant and quantization profile.
[01:50] Marcus: Is the quantization annotation coming from the runtime? We do mixed precision and want to understand perf differences.
[01:55] Priya: Yes, runtime emits which kernel profile was used; on Dedicated you'll see the selected kernel and sequence length bucketing.
[02:10] Sara: How frequent are traces sampled? We have high qps so full capture would be huge.
[02:15] Alex: Good point. Sampling policies are configurable — you can do deterministic sampling for errors and exceptions (100%), rate-based sampling for successes, or dynamic sampling based on latency thresholds. For pilot we'd suggest 100% for errors + 1% for success requests.
[02:35] Ben: And retention? Can we export logs off-cluster?
[02:38] Priya: Yes, request logs can be exported to S3 or your internal ELK/CloudWatch. Retention windows in the console control how long we keep them; in Dedicated you can set retention to match your policy or opt to forward immediately.
[02:52] Marcus: Ok show us error analysis.
[02:55] Priya: (switches view) Error analysis view groups failures by signature and shows sample requests. It does fuzzy grouping — similar to Sentry but optimized for inference errors, e.g., KV cache misses that lead to prefix latency, or model decode failures.
[03:12] [screen] Here's an example group: "decoder overflow" — you can click into the group to see top traces, aggregate token counts, and a replay of the request (if payload retained).
[03:30] Marcus: Can we redact fields before storing or in the UI? We can't have PHI in raw logs.
[03:35] Priya: Yes, field-level redaction at ingestion: regex-based or schema-based. There's also automatic PII detection with configurable rules. For air-gapped/private deployments you can opt-out of storing payloads entirely.
[03:50] Sara: For compliance, does the console keep an immutable audit trail of who looked at logs? We need that for audits.
[03:55] Alex: Audit logs track view events — who accessed which request id and when. We can forward these to your SIEM, and they're included in our SOC2 scope. We'll attach the SOC2 extract.
[04:12] Marcus: Can you show a live debugging flow, starting from an alert?
[04:15] Priya: Sure — step one, you click the alert and it links to the trace and request log. Step two, we show span level timelines with hoverable durations; step three, you can jump to related requests via correlated user_id or conversation_id.
[04:30] [Priya demos] Here's a trace where the model returned a malformed JSON — the error group shows 27 occurrences in the past hour, and the request log shows the prompt and the model response truncated.
[04:45] Marcus: Is there an easy way to correlate with upstream app logs?
[04:48] Priya: Yes, you can push a correlation id from your app in the request metadata and it'll appear in the trace. We also ingest external logs if you forward them so we can join on that ID.
[05:02] Sara: We have a strong requirement for data residency — logs must live in EU. Does Redwood support region-scoped retention?
[05:08] Alex: Yes — you can pin logs and traces to a region. Hosted offers region options; Dedicated/Private gives you full control. We'll provide region placement docs.
[05:20] Ben: Any limitations on log export rates? We might have bursts.
[05:24] Priya: There's throughput controls and backpressure — exports are asynchronous; for very high-volume customers we recommend streaming exports to a local collector in VPC to avoid backpressure.
[05:35] Marcus: Let's talk about debugging common failure modes — for example, tokenization mismatches we've seen.
[05:40] Priya: In the trace you'll see a 'tokenize' span. If tokenizer fails or produces unexpected tokens, the downstream decode span will error and we'll surface both. You can open the request and see the raw token ids if retained, or a diff view between expected vs actual output.
[05:58] [small digression] Alex: there's an internal note on the deck about how we handle model fallbacks; basically automatic fallback to a compatible model variant for timeouts.
[06:10] Marcus: How do rollouts affect tracing? If we do A/B, can we see traces by rollout?
[06:14] Priya: Yes, traces are tagged with rollout id and version; you can filter and compare error rates and latency across cohorts.
[06:25] Sara: If we run a canary and it shows elevated errors, can the console automatically route traffic away?
[06:29] Alex: We have automatic fallback policies and canary detection; you can configure automatic rollback or traffic rebalancing to avoid impacting production.
[06:40] Marcus: Great. On the security side, Ben asked about SSO and RBAC for the console.
[06:44] Ben: Yes, we use SAML; we also need fine-grained RBAC so that only a small group can see raw payloads.
[06:50] Priya: Redwood supports SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. RBAC is role-based and you can set a permission 'view raw payloads' separate from 'view traces'. Audit events capture who toggled these.
[07:08] Ben: Can we set a policy so that devs never see PHI but support engineers can?
[07:12] Alex: Yes, you can create roles for Support, Dev, Security and restrict the raw payload permission to Security.
[07:20] Marcus: Let's cover request logs format — what fields are included?
[07:24] Priya: We capture request_id, timestamp, model, route, client metadata, correlation ids, prompt length, token counts, latency breakdowns, and optional payload (redacted or full).
[07:36] Marcus: Is there a standardized schema export for SIEM integration?
[07:40] Priya: Exports are JSON with a documented schema, and we provide parsers for ELK/CloudWatch. We'll attach the schema link in the follow-up.
[07:52] [Priya shows an example log] The console has a log viewer with quick filters and the ability to construct saved queries. You can also run a replay against a sandbox model to reproduce.
[08:05] Marcus: That replay feature — does it call live models or a safe sandbox?
[08:08] Priya: Sandbox by default. For Dedicated you can configure a replay environment that mirrors your production model weights if you choose.
[08:20] Sara: Any latency added by tracing itself?
[08:23] Priya: Tracing is lightweight; spans are emitted asynchronously. For very sensitive low-latency flows you can disable certain spans or use sampling.
[08:36] Marcus: Ok show us a concrete debugging example end-to-end.
[08:40] Priya: (demo) Alert fired for increased "decoder overflow". From the alert, we jump to the top group, then pick a recent trace. You can see a spike in 'model decode' span at 2.3s. Expanding the request log shows an unexpected token sequence and the response cutoff.
[09:00] Marcus: Can we annotate traces with our internal ticket id so triage is easier?
[09:04] Priya: Yes, you can add annotations or link a ticket via URL — it's in the trace metadata.
[09:15] Ben: About retention — do you support tiered retention so that metadata is kept longer than payloads?
[09:20] Alex: Yes, metadata can be kept long-term and payloads short-term. We recommend keeping metadata for 1 year for analytics and reducing payload retention to your compliance window.
[09:35] Marcus: On the pilot, we'd like a week of full tracing for errors and 5% of success requests to validate. Do you have a cost estimate?
[09:42] Alex: We'll model that — for 10M monthly tokens with that sampling, we can provide a Dedicated pilot quote. We'll include the math in the follow-up.
[09:55] [noise, crosstalk]
[10:05] Priya: A couple of advanced notes: automatic KV cache warmup traces and cross-request prefix caching are annotated so you can see cache hits vs misses; that often explains token gen latency. Also for quantized models we surface quantization-grade and any fallback to fp16 kernels.
[10:25] Marcus: Nice. Are there common misconfigurations you see?
[10:29] Priya: Yes: 1) insufficient sampling so errors are missed; 2) not forwarding logs to a local collector in VPC causing export delays; 3) confusion between model rollouts and routing policies. We try to detect and warn about these in the console.
[10:45] Sara: Could you provide a brief runbook template for triage? That helps our on-call.
[10:50] Alex: We'll include a runbook template and a checklist for triage steps.
[11:00] Marcus: Quick question — if we disable payload retention, does error analysis still work?
[11:04] Priya: Error grouping still works because we use signatures derived from metadata and model error codes; sample replays require payloads.
[11:15] Ben: For SOC2, do you provide a shared responsibility matrix?
[11:18] Alex: Yes, we'll include the SRM in the follow-up security pack.
[11:28] Marcus: Anything else on tracing?
[11:31] Priya: We also have trace-level annotations for model version and compile-time kernel. Makes it easier to pinpoint regressions after model updates.
[11:40] Marcus: Good. Let's talk timeline — we want to run a pilot mid-October and decide by early November.
[11:45] Alex: Sounds doable. We'll send pricing and the pilot onboarding doc.
[11:52] [wrap up] Alex: Recap: we'll send SOC2/KMS/HSM docs, the SIEM/schema link, pilot quote and runbook. Priya will prepare the benchmark harness. Marcus to share error samples and retention requirements.
[12:05] Marcus: Thanks all, that covers it.
[12:08] Alex: Thanks everyone — recording and console access link to follow.

End of transcript. Note: transcription includes minor mis-hearings ("K V cash" for KV cache, occasional speaker label swaps).
